newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tajik clashes worry Russia, intervention unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Tajik clashes worry Russia, intervention unlikely.

text.p: A flare-up of violence in Tajikistan is a nightmare for Russia which carries the risk of Moscow being sucked into a new conflict on its southern fringes.

But the bitter lessons learned from the disastrous interventions in Afghanistan in 1979 and Chechnya in 1994 make a Russian military campaign unlikely in Tajikistan, despite the threat of instability spreading to Russia.
Moscow reacted cautiously to the fighting which erupted in Tajikistan at the weekend.

"Experience of Tajikistan shows that any hasty measures can only aggravate the situation and lead to very serious complications," Russian Foreign Ministry official Valery Nesterushkin told Interfax news agency on Monday.
"We hope that Tajikistan, worn out by this lengthy conflict, will find the strength to avoid the development of the regrettably traditional scenario typical of this region."

Moscow has long been worried that Islamic fundamentalism, illegal arms, more drugs and chaos could seep through its "soft underbelly" from Central Asia and has tried to remain an active player in the region since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Russia played a major role in mediating talks between the Tajik government and Islamist opposition forces which led to a peace deal in June which ended four years of civil war.
It has 20,000 troops in Tajikistan carrying out peacekeeping duties and guarding borders, including the often-breached frontier with Afghanistan.
The presence of the Russian soldiers helped ensure President Imomali Rakhmonov emerged from the civil war on top and they are widely regarded as shoring up his shaky hold in power now.

Doing so helps Russian keep some influence in Central Asia and is part of efforts to tighten up the Commonwealth of Independent States with Russia playing a pivotal role in the 12-nation alliance, set up on the ashes of the Soviet Union.
Vladimir Lukin, head of Russian parliament's foreign affairs committee, said Moscow should do its utmost to help Tajikistan but that it would be a mistake to intervene militarily.
"It would mean bloodshed," he said in an interview with Ekho Moskvy radio. "I think we have to step up our actions (but) on the diplomatic front."

Representatives of the peacekeepers tried to negotiate between the rival armed groups who started the new violence by fighting in northern Dushanbe on Saturday. The Russians have not been involved in the latest fighting.

The Russians tasted success in the negotiations between the government and the Islamist opposition but appear at sea in dealing with the nominally pro-government warlords who have established fiefdoms which undermine Rakhmonov's authority.
"The Russians are at a loss. They understand fighting between the government and the Islamists but the fighting inside the government foxes them," a Western diplomat said.
"With its drubbing in Chechnya only just behind it, the Kremlin is unlikely to want to wade into a war in far-flung Central Asia."

Russian troops withdrew from Chechnya a year ago after a 21-month conflict in which separatist guerrillas humiliated them. The decade-long intervention in Afghanistan was a debacle in which Moscow said more than 13,000 Soviet soldiers died.
Independent Russian analysts say they hope Moscow has drawn the proper conclusions form Chechnya and Afghanistan.
"I see few options for Russia in Tajikistan except to get involved as little as possible," said Andrei Piontkovsky, head of Moscow's Centre for Strategic Studies.
